readings.c1s1:
{{smaller|'''Unlimited function.''' See ''function.''—'''Unlimited problem''', in ''math.'', a problem which may have an infinite number of solutions.—'''Unlimited quantity.''' See ''quantity.''}}

'''unlimitedly''' (un-lim′i-ted-li), ''adv.'' In an unlimited manner or degree.

'''unlimitedness''' (un-lim′i-ted-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unlimited or boundless, or of being undefined.

'''unline''' (un-līn′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''line''<sup>3</sup>.] To take the lining out of; hence, to empty. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|It ''unlines'' their purses.
{{right|''Davies'', Bienvenu, p. 6. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unlineal''' (un-lin′ē̤-al), ''a.'' Not lineal; not coming in the order of succession. ''Shak.'', Macbeth, iii. 1. 63.

'''unlining''' (un-lī′ning), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''unline'', ''v.''] In ''bot.'', Lindley’s name for the process of chorization or chorisis, the ''dédoublement'' (deduplication) of Dunal. See ''chorisis.''

'''unlink''' (un-lingk′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''link''<sup>1</sup>.] To separate the links of; loose, as something fastened by a link; unfasten; untwist; uncoil.
{{smaller block|Seeing Orlando, it [a snake] ''unlinked'' itself.
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, iv. 3. 112.}}
<poem>I cannot mount till thou ''unlink'' my chains;
I cannot come till thou release my bands.</poem>
{{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, v. 9.}}}}

'''unlinked''' (un-lingkt′), ''a.'' Not connected by or as by links. ''J. Martineau'', Materialism, p. 127.

'''unliquefied''' (un-lik′wẹ̄-fīd), ''a.'' Unmelted; not dissolved. ''Addison'', Travels in Italy.

'''unliquidated''' (un-lik′wi-dā-ted), ''a.'' Not liquidated; not settled; unadjusted: as, an ''unliqui-''
readings.c1s2:
''dated'' debt; ''unliquidated'' accounts. See ''liquidate.''—'''Unliquidated damages.''' {{smaller|See ''damage''.}}

¶
'''unliquored''' (un-lik′ọrd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not moistened or smeared with liquor; not lubricated; dry. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Churches and states, like an ''unliquored'' coach, . . . on fire with their own motion.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Sermons.}}}}
'''2.''' Not filled with liquor; not in liquor; not intoxicated; sober. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|I doubt me whether the very sobernesse of such a one, like an ''unlicour’d'' Silenus, were not stark drunk.
{{right|''Milton'', Apology for Smectymnuus.}}}}

'''unlistening''' (un-lis′ning), ''a.'' Not listening; not hearing; not regarding or heeding. ''Thomson'', Liberty.

'''unliturgize''' (un-lit′ėr-jīz), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''liturg-y'' + ''-ize.''] To deprive of a liturgy. ''Bp. Gauden'', Tears of the Church, p. 609. (''Davies.'') [Rare.]

'''unlive<sup>1</sup>''' (un-liv′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''live''<sup>1</sup>.] To live in a manner contrary to; annul or undo by living.
{{smaller block|We must ''unlive'' our former lives.
{{right|''Glanville'', Vanity of Dogmatizing, viii.}}}}

'''unlive<sup>2</sup>†''' (un-līv′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''life'' (cf. ''alive'', ''live''<sup>2</sup>).] To bereave or deprive of life.
{{smaller block|<poem>If in the child the father’s image lies,
Where shall I live now Lucrece is ''unlived?''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 1754.}}}}

'''unliveliness''' (un-līv′li-nes), ''n.'' Want of liveliness; dullness; heaviness. ''Milton'', Divorce, i. 3.

'''unload''' (un-lōd′), ''v.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''load''<sup>2</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To take the load from; discharge of a load
readings.c1s3:
or cargo; disburden: as, to ''unload'' a ship; to ''unload'' a cart.—'''2.''' To remove, as a cargo or burden, from a vessel, vehicle, or the like; discharge: as, to ''unload'' freight.—'''3.''' Figuratively, to relieve from anything onerous or troublesome; remove and cause to cease to be burdensome.
{{smaller block|Nor can my tongue ''unload'' my heart’s great burthen.
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., ii. 1. 81.}}
<poem>From this high theme how can I part,
Ere half ''unloaded'' is my heart!</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Marmion, Int. to i.}}}}
'''4.''' To withdraw the charge, as of powder and shot or ball, from: as, to ''unload'' a gun.—'''5.''' To sell in large quantities, as stock; get rid of: as, to ''unload'' shares of the A and B railway. [Colloq.]

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To go through the process of unloading; discharge a cargo.
{{smaller block|No ship could ''unload'' in any bay or estuary which he [the king] had not declared to be a port.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., xviii.}}}}

'''unloader''' (un-lō′dėr), ''n.'' One who or that which unloads; specifically, a contrivance for unloading, as hay. ''The Engineer'', LXVIII. 199.

'''unloading-block''' (un-lō′ding-blok), ''n.'' In ''sugar-manuf.'', a bench on which the mold containing a sugar-loaf is inverted, and on which the sugar is left standing until removed to the drying-room.
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become unfastened; fall in pieces; lose all connection or union.

{{smaller block|Without this virtue, the publick union must ''unloose'', the strength decay, and the pleasure grow faint.
{{right|''Jeremy Collier.''}}}}

'''unloosen''' (un-lö′sn), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> (here intensive) + ''loosen.''] To unloose; loosen. ''V. Knox'', Essays, ii.

'''unlord''' (un-lôrd′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''lord.''] To deprive of the title, rank, and dignity of a lord; reduce or degrade from a peer to a commoner. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|The worst and strangest of that Any thing which the people demanded was but the ''unlording'' of Bishops, and expelling them the House. ''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, vi.
<poem>
So, after that,
We had to dis-archbishop and ''unlord'',
And make you simple Cranmer once again.
</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Queen Mary, ii. 2.}}}}

'''unlorded''' (un-lôr′ded), ''a.'' Not raised or preferred to the rank of a lord. ''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., i.

'''unlordly''' (un-lôrd′li), ''a.'' Not lordly; not arbitrary. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|The Pastorlike and Apostolik imitation of meeke and ''unlordly'' Discipline. ''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., ii.}}

'''unlosable''' (un-lö′za-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being lost. Also ''unloseable.'' [Rare.]

{{smaller block|The Epicureans . . . ascribe to every particular atom an innate and ''unloseable'' mobility. ''Boyle'', Works, I. 445.}}

'''unliquefied''' (un-lik′wẹ̄-fīd), ''a.'' Unmelted; not dissolved. ''Addison'', Travels in Italy.

'''unliquidated''' (un-lik′wi-dā-ted), ''a.'' Not liquidated; not settled; unadjusted: as, an ''unliquidated'' debt; ''unliquidated'' accounts. See ''liquidate.''—'''Unliquidated damages.''' {{smaller|See ''damage''.}}

{{smaller block|We must ''unlive'' our former lives.
{{right|''Glanville'', Vanity of Dogmatizing, viii.}}}}

'''unlive<sup>2</sup>†''' (un-līv′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''life'' (cf. ''alive'', ''live''<sup>2</sup>).] To bereave or deprive of life.

Where shall I live now Lucrece is ''unlived?''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 1754.}}}}

'''unliveliness''' (un-līv′li-nes), ''n.'' Want of liveliness; dullness; heaviness. ''Milton'', Divorce, i. 3.

'''unload''' (un-lōd′), ''v.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''load''<sup>2</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To take the load from; discharge of a load or cargo; disburden: as, to ''unload'' a ship; to ''unload'' a cart.—'''2.''' To remove, as a cargo or burden, from a vessel, vehicle, or the like; discharge: as, to ''unload'' freight.—'''3.''' Figuratively, to relieve from anything onerous or troublesome; remove and cause to cease to be burdensome.
{{smaller block|Nor can my tongue ''unload'' my heart’s great burthen.
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., ii. 1. 81.}}
<poem>From this high theme how can I part,
Ere half ''unloaded'' is my heart!</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Marmion, Int. to i.}}}}
'''4.''' To withdraw the charge, as of powder and shot or ball, from: as, to ''unload'' a gun.—'''5.''' To sell in large quantities, as stock; get rid of: as, to ''unload'' shares of the A and B railway. [Colloq.]

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To go through the process of unloading; discharge a cargo.
{{smaller block|No ship could ''unload'' in any bay or estuary which he [the king] had not declared to be a port.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., xviii.}}}}

'''unloader''' (un-lō′dėr), ''n.'' One who or that which unloads; specifically, a contrivance for unloading, as hay. ''The Engineer'', LXVIII. 199.

'''unloading-block''' (un-lō′ding-blok), ''n.'' In ''sugar-manuf.'', a bench on which the mold containing a sugar-loaf is inverted, and on which the sugar is left standing until removed to the drying-room.

'''unloading-machine''' (un-lō′ding-mạ-shēn″), ''n.'' An apparatus for unloading freight from boats, cars, and wagons. {{smaller|The most usual form is a sort of elevator consisting of a series of cups or buckets carried by an endless band. ''E. H. Knight.''}}

'''unlocated''' (un-lō′kā-ted), ''a.'' Not located or placed; specifically, in the United States, not surveyed and marked off: said of land. See ''locate'', 2.
{{smaller block|The disposal of the ''unlocated'' lands will hereafter be a valuable source of revenue, and an immediate one of credit.
{{right|''A. Hamilton'', The Continentalist, No. 6.}}}}

'''unlock''' (un-lok′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''unlouken'', ''onlouken'' (pret. ''unlek'', pp. ''unloken'', ''unloke''), < AS. ''unlūcan'', unlock, < ''un-'', back, + ''lūcan'', lock: see ''un-''<sup>2</sup> and ''lock''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' To unfasten, as something which has been locked; open, as what has been shut, closed in, or protected by a lock: as, to ''unlock'' a door or a chest.
{{smaller block|I have seen her . . . ''unlock'' her closet.
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, v. 1. 6.}}
<poem>Go in; there are the keys, ''unlock'' his fetters;
And arm ye nobly both.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Double Marriage, ii. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' To open, in general; lay open.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thou ’st ''unlocked''
A tongue was vowed to silence.</poem>
{{right|''Ford'', Lover’s Melancholy, ii. 1.}}
Saturday Morning, as soon as my Senses are ''unlocked'', I get up.
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. vi. 32.}}}}
'''3†.''' To spread out.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Vnlouke'' hus legges abrod, other lygge at hus ese,
Reste hym, and roste hym and his ryg turne,
Drynke drue and deepe and drawe hym thanne to bedde.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), x. 143.}}}}

'''4.''' To disclose; reveal; make known.
{{smaller block|That sweven hath Daniel ''unloke.''
{{right|''Gower,'' Conf. Amant., Prol.}}}}

'''unlocked''' (un-lokt′), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''locked,'' pp. of ''lock''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] Not locked.

'''unlodge''' (un-loj′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''lodge.''] To deprive of a lodging; dislodge. ''Carew.''

'''unlogical''' (un-loj′i-kạl), ''a.'' Illogical. ''Fuller,'' Worthies, Kent, i. 487. (''Davies.'')

'''unlook''' (un-lu̇k′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''look''<sup>1</sup>.] To recall or retract, as a look. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|He . . . turned his eyes towards me, then from me, as if he would ''unlook'' his own looks.
{{right|''Richardson,'' Clarissa Harlowe, V. 215.}}}}

'''unlooked''' (un-lu̇kt′), ''a.'' Not expected or anticipated: rare except in the phrase ''unlooked for.''
{{smaller block|By some ''unlook’d'' accident cut off!
{{right|''Shak.,'' Rich. III., i. 3. 214.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Unlooked for,''' not looked for; not sought or searched for; not expected; not foreseen; not anticipated.}}
{{smaller block|An accident ''unlook’d for'' put new counsels into thir minds.
{{right|''Milton,'' Hist. Eng., ii.}}}}

'''unloose''' (un-lös′), ''v.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> (here intensive) + ''loose.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To loose; unfasten; untie; undo; unravel.
{{smaller block|The Gordian knot of it he will ''unloose.''
{{right|''Shak.,'' Hen. V., i. 1. 46.}}}}

'''2.''' To let go or free from hold or fastening; unbind from bonds, fetters, cords, or the like; set at liberty; release.
{{smaller block|<poem>Where I am robb’d and bound,
There must I be ''unloosed.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.,'' Hen. VIII., ii. 4. 147.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become unfastened; fall in pieces; lose all connection or union.

{{smaller block|Without this virtue, the publick union must ''unloose'', the strength decay, and the pleasure grow faint.
{{right|''Jeremy Collier.''}}}}

'''unloosen''' (un-lö′sn), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> (here intensive) + ''loosen.''] To unloose; loosen. ''V. Knox'', Essays, ii.

'''unlord''' (un-lôrd′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''lord.''] To deprive of the title, rank, and dignity of a lord; reduce or degrade from a peer to a commoner. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|The worst and strangest of that Any thing which the people demanded was but the ''unlording'' of Bishops, and expelling them the House. ''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, vi.}}
<poem>
So, after that,
We had to dis-archbishop and ''unlord'',
And make you simple Cranmer once again.
</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', Queen Mary, ii. 2.}}}}

'''unlorded''' (un-lôr′ded), ''a.'' Not raised or preferred to the rank of a lord. ''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., i.

'''unlordly''' (un-lôrd′li), ''a.'' Not lordly; not arbitrary. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|The Pastorlike and Apostolik imitation of meeke and ''unlordly'' Discipline. ''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., ii.}}

'''unlosable''' (un-lö′za-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being lost. Also ''unloseable.'' [Rare.]

{{smaller block|The Epicureans . . . ascribe to every particular atom an innate and ''unloseable'' mobility. ''Boyle'', Works, I. 445.}}

'''unlost''' (un-lôst′), ''a.'' Not lost. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|A paradise ''unlost.'' {{right|''Young'', Night Thoughts, ix. 1071.}}}}

'''unlove''' (un-luv′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''unloven''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> (in second quot. ''un-''<sup>2</sup>) + ''love''<sup>1</sup>.] Not to love; to cease to love. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>I ne kan nor may
For al this world withinne myn herte fynde
To ''unloven'' you a quarter of a day.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, v. 1698.}}
I had learnt to love Mr. Rochester; I could not ''unlove'' him now. {{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Jane Eyre, xviii.}}}}

'''unlove''' (un′luv), ''n.'' The absence of love; hate. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|''Unlove'' began its work even in the Apostles’ times. {{right|''Pusey'', Eirenicon, p. 62.}}}}

'''unloved''' (un-luvd′), ''a.'' Not loved. ''Chaucer.''

'''unloveliness''' (un-luv′li-nes), ''n.'' Lack of loveliness. {{smaller|(''a'') Unamiableness; lack of the qualities which attract love.}}
{{smaller block|The old man . . . followed his suit with all means . . . that might help to countervail his own ''unloveliness.'' {{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, ii.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Want of beauty or attractiveness to the eye; plainness of feature or appearance.}}

'''unlovely''' (un-luv′li), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unlovelich''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''lovely''.] Not lovely. {{smaller|(''a'') Not amiable; destitute of the qualities which attract love, or possessing qualities that excite dislike; disagreeable.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I love thee, all ''unlovely'' as thou seem’st
And dreaded as thou art! ''Cowper'', Task, iv. 128.</poem>}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Not beautiful or attractive to the eye; displeasing to the sight.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Dark house, by which once more I stand
Here in the long ''unlovely'' street.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, vii.}}}}

'''unloving''' (un-luv′ing), ''a.'' Not loving; not fond; unkind. ''J. Udall'', On Ephesians, Prol.

'''unlovingness''' (un-luv′ing-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unloving.
{{smaller block|Time and its austere experience of the outer world’s ''unlovingness'' have made her thankfully take affection’s clasp. {{right|''R. Broughton'', Joan, II. xi.}}}}

'''unluckful†''' (un-luk′fu̇l), ''a.'' Bringing ill luck; mischievous.
{{smaller block|O Pallas, ladie of citees, why settest thou thy delite in three the moste ''vnluckefull'' beastes of the worlde, the oulette, the dragon, and the people? {{right|''Udall'', tr. of Apophthegms of Erasmus, p. 375. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unluckily''' (un-luk′i-li), ''adv.'' In an unlucky or unfortunate manner; unfortunately; unhappily; by ill luck.
{{smaller block|Was there ever so prosperous an invention thus ''unluckily'' perverted and spoiled by a . . . book-worm, a candle-waster? {{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia’s Revels, iii. 2.}}
I was once in a mixt assembly that was full of noise and mirth, when on a sudden an old woman ''unluckily'' observed there were thirteen of us in company. {{right|''Addison'', Omens.}}}}

'''unluckiness''' (un-luk′i-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unlucky, in any sense.

'''unlucky''' (un-luk′i), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not lucky or fortunate; not favored by fortune; unsuccessful; subject to frequent misfortune, failure, or mishap; ill-fated; unfortunate; unhappy.
{{smaller block|In short, they were ''unlucky'' to have been bred in an unpolished age, and more ''unlucky'' to live to a refined one. {{right|''Dryden'', Def. of Epil. to 2d pt. Conq. Granada.}}}}
'''2.''' Not resulting in success; resulting in failure, disaster, or misfortune. {{smaller block|''Unlucky'' accidents which make such experiments miscarry.{{right|''Boyle.''}}}}
'''3.''' Accompanied by or bringing misfortune, disappointment, disaster, or the like; ill-omened; inauspicious.
{{smaller block|A most ''unlucky'' hour.{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., ii. 3. 251.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Haunt me not with that ''unlucky'' face.</poem>{{right|''Dryden'', Aurengzebe, iv. 1.}}}}
'''4.''' Mischievous; mischievously waggish. [Archaic.]
{{smaller block|Why, cries an ''unlucky'' wag, a less bag might have served.{{right|''Sir R. L’Estrange.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>There was a lad, th’ ''unluckiest'' of his crew,
Was still contriving something bad but new.</poem>{{right|''Dr. W. King.''}}}}

'''unlust†''', ''n.'' [< ME. ''unlust'', < AS. ''unlust'', displeasure, dislike (= OHG. ''unlust'', MHG. G. ''unlust'', displeasure, = Icel. ''úlyst'', bad appetite, = Sw. ''olyst'' = Dan. ''ulyst'' = Goth. ''unlustus''), < ''un-'', not, + ''lust'', pleasure: see ''lust''<sup>1</sup>.] Displeasure; dislike.
{{smaller block|He dooth alle thyng . . . with ydelnesse and ''unlust.''{{right|''Chaucer'', Parson’s Tale.}}}}

'''unlustrous''' (un-lus′trus), ''a.'' Not lustrous; not shining.
{{smaller block|<poem>In an eye
Base and ''unlustrous'' as the smoky light
That ’s fed with stinking tallow.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, i. 6. 109.}}}}
{{smaller block|[The above is the reading in some modern editions; the old editions have ''illustrious.'']}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
